zh.title: 惡念、憤怒的念頭怎麼停：佛陀的五個步驟（《息止尋念經》MN 20）
zh.seo_title: 負面念頭停不下來？佛陀教的 5 個步驟：《息止尋念經》MN 20 原典解說
zh.seo_description: 一直想不好的事、憤怒或惡念揮之不去、胡思亂想停不下來？《息止尋念經》（MN 20）記載佛陀教的五步驟遞進對治法：換上善的對象、看清念頭的過患、不去理會、放緩念頭的推力，真的沒辦法時才咬牙以心制心。本頁依巴利原文逐段解說這五個方法與它們的次序。
zh.question: 一直有負面念頭、停不下來，佛教有辦法處理嗎？
zh.definition: 《息止尋念經》（Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta，MN 20）教的「五步驟遞進對治法」：當貪、瞋、癡相關的「惡不善念」（pāpakā akusalā vitakkā）生起時，依序換用五種方法——（1）換上一個善的對象、（2）審視念頭的過患、（3）不念不作意（不去理會）、（4）放緩念頭的推力、（5）咬牙以心制心——由溫和到強硬層層遞進，前一個方法奏效就不必用到後面，終點是對自己的念頭得自在。

sections.heading: 背景：上心修習與五種「相」
paragraphs: 《息止尋念經》（Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta，MN 20，直譯《尋的安立經》）是一部專門講「念頭怎麼停」的經。一開場，佛陀對從事「上心修習」（adhicitta，指靜坐、修定的功夫）的比丘說：應當適時在心裡「作意五種相」——也就是備妥五種對治念頭的方法。這裡的「相」（nimitta）指的是心所緣、心去注意的對象或方式。
要對治的是什麼？是「惡的不善尋」（pāpakā akusalā vitakkā）——經文一再點名它們與「欲、瞋、癡」相應，也就是被貪求、憤怒、迷惑帶起來的那一類念頭。憤怒的念頭、揮之不去的惡念、一直想不好的事，正落在這個範圍內。以下五個方法是有次序的：從最溫和的換念頭，一路遞進到最激烈的硬壓；前一個奏效，就不必動用後面的。

sections.heading: 方法一：換上一個善的對象
paragraphs: 第一個方法：當你依著某個對象、去注意它時，冒出了貪瞋癡相關的壞念頭，那就「捨掉那個相，改去作意另一個與善相應的相」。白話說，就是把注意力從勾起惡念的對象上移開，換上一個良善的對象——像是換一個念頭、換一件正向的事來想。經文說，這樣一換，那些惡的不善念就會被捨棄、消逝，心於是在自身內部安住、沉澱、成為一境而入定。
佛陀用木工的比喻收尾：一位熟練的木匠，會用一根細小的釘子，把嵌著的粗大釘子頂出來、換掉。善念之於惡念，就像那根細釘——不是硬拔，而是用一個東西頂替掉另一個。這是五法裡最溫和、也最該先試的一招。

sections.heading: 方法二：看清念頭的過患
paragraphs: 如果換了對象、惡念照樣冒出來，就進到第二個方法：「審視那些念頭的過患」。怎麼審視？經文給了現成的念白：「這些念頭是不善的，這些念頭是有過失的，這些念頭招致苦果。」也就是不再被念頭牽著跑，而是退一步盯著它、看清它會帶來什麼壞處。經文說，這樣審視之後，那些惡不善念便被捨斷、消逝，心在內部安住入定。
佛陀的比喻很強烈：一個愛好裝飾的年輕男女，若脖子上被掛了蛇、狗或人的死屍，一定又厭惡、又羞恥、又嫌惡，急著把它甩開。看清惡念的過患，就會像面對那具死屍一樣——不必勉強自己討厭它，看清楚了，自然就想擺脫。

sections.heading: 方法三：不去理會、不作意
paragraphs: 第三個方法：連過患都審視了，念頭還在，那就對它們「不念、不作意」（asatiamanasikāra）——不去回想、不去理會、不給它注意力。這不是硬壓，而是不餵養：既然一直投注心思只會讓念頭燒得更旺，那就乾脆把心思從它身上挪開。經文說，這樣不理會之後，那些惡不善念同樣被捨斷、消逝，心得安住入定。
佛陀的比喻是：一個視力正常的人，若不想看見眼前的東西，他大可閉上眼睛，或把目光轉向別處。對治不斷冒出來的念頭也一樣——不必和它四目相對、正面糾纏，把注意力挪開就好。

sections.heading: 方法四：放緩念頭背後的推力
paragraphs: 第四個方法比較細緻。若不理會還是沒用，就去「作意那些念頭的尋思行之靜止」（vitakkasaṅkhārasaṇṭhāna）——留意並放緩推著念頭跑的那股力道。經文說，這樣作意之後，那些惡不善念便被捨斷、消逝，心得安住入定。
佛陀的比喻是一個快步走的人：他會問自己「我幹嘛走這麼快？」於是改成慢走；再問一次，於是站住；再問，於是坐下；再問，於是躺下——一路從粗重的動作姿態，換成越來越微細的姿態。念頭也是如此：不是硬把它掐斷，而是一層層降低它的力道與粗猛，讓奔騰的念頭慢下來、鬆下來，最後自然平息。

sections.heading: 方法五：咬牙以心制心（最後手段）
paragraphs: 第五個、也是最後一個方法，是硬碰硬。前四個都試過、念頭仍死纏不放，佛陀才教：「咬緊牙關，以舌頂住上顎，以心制伏心，用力壓下、徹底折伏。」這是最激烈的手段，靠的是意志力。經文說，這樣強力制伏之後，那些惡不善念被捨斷、消逝，心得安住入定。
佛陀的比喻是：一個強壯的人，抓住較為羸弱的人的頭、頸或肩，強行制伏、壓下去。要留意的是，這是壓軸、不是首選——經文把它排在第五，正說明前面較溫和的方法都應先試；真的無計可施，才動用意志力硬壓。

sections.heading: 五步的共同原理與實修提醒
paragraphs: 把五個方法擺在一起看，共同的原理很清楚。第一，對治的對象始終是同一類——貪、瞋、癡帶起的「惡不善念」；第二，每個方法奏效的標準也一樣：那些念頭被捨棄、消逝，心於是「在自身內部安住、沉澱、成為一境而入定」；第三，五者是遞進的，從換對象、看過患、不理會、放緩力道，到最後咬牙硬壓，一層比一層用力，前一招管用就不必動用後一招。
經文最後說，能這樣純熟運用五法的比丘，就是「念頭之道上的自在者」：他想要哪個念頭就起哪個，不想要就不起——徹底斬斷了渴愛、解開了結縛，作了苦的終結。實修上這給了兩個提醒：一是別死守單一招式，A 招無效就換 B 招，這本來就是佛陀設計的用法；二是「咬牙硬壓」是最後手段、不是日常做法，多數時候，換個對象或不去理會，念頭就鬆開了。

zh.mahayana_note: 這五步對治法是止觀實修的具體技術。後世佛教各傳統，都在「如何對治妄念」上有各自的開展——例如以稱名念佛、持咒、觀想、參話頭等法門來收攝紛飛的念頭，或在近代內觀傳統中以「標記」（noting）的方式覺察念頭的生滅。這些是後世的方法開展與詮釋；本頁只呈現《息止尋念經》巴利原文所教的五個步驟，不對各家方法的高下或教義取向做裁決。

faq.q: 一直有負面念頭、停不下來，佛教怎麼辦？
faq.a: 《息止尋念經》（MN 20）正是為此而說。佛陀教了五個由淺到深的步驟：（1）把注意力從勾起惡念的對象移開，換上一個良善的對象；（2）看清這些念頭的過患——它們不善、有過失、招致苦果；（3）乾脆不去理會、不作意，不給它注意力；（4）放緩推著念頭跑的力道，讓它慢下來；（5）真的沒辦法時，才咬牙以心制心、用意志力硬壓。前一步奏效，就不必用到後一步。

faq.q: 《息止尋念經》的五個方法是哪五個？
faq.a: 依經文次序：一、捨掉勾起惡念的相，改作意另一個「與善相應的相」（換對象）；二、審視那些念頭的過患，念著「這些念頭不善、有過失、招致苦果」；三、對那些念頭「不念、不作意」（不去理會）；四、作意「尋思之行的靜止」（vitakkasaṅkhārasaṇṭhāna，放緩念頭背後的推力）；五、咬緊牙關、以舌抵上顎，「以心制伏心」，強力壓下。五者由溫和到強硬遞進使用。

faq.q: 打坐時雜念太多、靜不下來，可以用嗎？
faq.a: 可以。經文開宗明義就是對從事「上心修習」（adhicitta，即修定、靜坐）的人說的，正是為了坐中雜念而設。靜坐時若冒出貪瞋癡相關的念頭，可依序試：先把注意力換到善的所緣（例如回到呼吸或善念），不行就審視這些雜念的過患，再不行就不去理它，接著放緩它的力道，最後才用意志力硬攝。每個方法奏效的判準都是同一個：念頭消退、心安住成一境而入定。

faq.q: 一直想不好的事、惡念揮之不去，是不是我很糟？
faq.a: 經文把貪瞋癡相關的念頭當作「可對治」的對象，而不是道德污點——它連對正在修定的比丘都會生起，佛陀因此才給了五套辦法。換句話說，念頭冒出來不代表你這個人壞，重點在於你有沒有方法處理它。這五步就是一套具體、可操作的處理流程，從溫和到強力，總有一招能讓念頭鬆開。

faq.q: 這五個方法有先後順序嗎？可以只用一個嗎？
faq.a: 有明確順序，而且是「遞進」的：經文每一步都說「若前一個方法用了、念頭仍然生起」，才進到下一步。所以如果第一招（換對象）就有效，念頭消退、心安住入定，你完全可以只用它，不必往下走。越後面的方法越用力，「咬牙以心制心」排在最末，是留給前面都無效時的最後手段。

en.title: How to Stop Angry or Negative Thoughts: the Buddha's Five Steps (MN 20)
en.seo_title: Negative Thoughts Won't Stop? The Buddha's 5 Steps — MN 20 Explained
en.seo_description: Can't stop dwelling on bad things, angry or unwholesome thoughts that won't go away, a mind that won't quiet down? The Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta (MN 20) records the Buddha's five-step, escalating method: switch to a wholesome object, see the drawbacks, ignore them, slow their momentum, and only as a last resort restrain mind with mind. This page explains the five methods and their order from the Pali text.
en.question: Can Buddhism help when negative thoughts just won't stop?
en.definition: The five-step, progressive method taught in the Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta (MN 20): when evil, unwholesome thoughts (pāpakā akusalā vitakkā) connected with greed, hatred, or delusion arise, the practitioner applies five techniques in order—(1) switch attention to a wholesome object, (2) examine the drawbacks of the thoughts, (3) give them no attention, (4) slow the driving force behind them, and (5) as a last resort, restrain mind with mind by clenching the teeth. Each step is used only if the gentler one before it fails; the goal is mastery over one's own thoughts.

sections.heading: Background: higher-mind training and the five "signs"
paragraphs: The Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta (MN 20, literally "The Discourse on the Stilling of Thought") is a text devoted precisely to the question of how to stop unwanted thoughts. At the outset, the Buddha tells a monk devoted to "the higher mind" (adhicitta—the work of meditation and concentration) that he should, from time to time, attend to "five signs"—that is, keep five methods ready for dealing with thoughts. Here a "sign" (nimitta) means the object the mind takes up, or the way it attends.

What is to be countered? The "evil, unwholesome thoughts" (pāpakā akusalā vitakkā)—which the text repeatedly names as connected with greed, hatred, and delusion; that is, thoughts driven by craving, anger, or confusion. Angry thoughts, unwholesome thoughts that won't go away, endlessly dwelling on bad things—all fall within this range. The five methods that follow are sequential: from the gentlest, swapping the thought, escalating to the most forceful, sheer suppression. If an earlier one works, there is no need to reach for the later ones.

sections.heading: Method one: switch to a wholesome object
paragraphs: The first method: when, in attending to some object, thoughts connected with greed, hatred, or delusion arise, then "abandon that sign and attend instead to another sign connected with the wholesome." In plain terms, move your attention off the object that provokes the bad thought and put a wholesome object in its place—switch to a different, positive thing to dwell on. The text says that with this switch, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and fade away, and the mind settles internally, quiets, becomes unified, and enters concentration.

The Buddha closes with the simile of the carpenter: a skilled carpenter uses a fine peg to knock out and replace a coarse one. A wholesome thought is to an unwholesome one as that fine peg—not yanked out by force, but displaced by substituting one thing for another. This is the gentlest of the five, and the one to try first.

sections.heading: Method two: see the drawbacks of the thoughts
paragraphs: If switching the object doesn't help and the bad thoughts keep coming, move to the second method: "examine the drawbacks of those thoughts." How? The text gives ready-made words: "These thoughts are unwholesome, these thoughts are blameworthy, these thoughts result in suffering." That is, instead of being dragged along by the thought, step back and look hard at it, seeing clearly the harm it brings. With this examination, the text says, the evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and fade, and the mind settles into concentration.

The Buddha's simile is vivid: a young man or woman fond of adornment, with the carcass of a snake, a dog, or a person hung around the neck, would be horrified, ashamed, and disgusted, eager to throw it off. Seeing the drawbacks of an unwholesome thought works the same way—you needn't force yourself to hate it; once you see it clearly, the wish to be rid of it comes on its own.

sections.heading: Method three: give it no attention
paragraphs: The third method: even after examining the drawbacks, if the thoughts remain, then toward them practice "non-recollection and non-attention" (asatiamanasikāra)—do not recall them, do not engage them, give them no attention. This is not forceful suppression but withholding fuel: since pouring attention on a thought only makes it burn hotter, simply take your mind off it. With this, the text says, the evil, unwholesome thoughts too are abandoned and fade, and the mind settles into concentration.

The Buddha's simile: a person with good eyesight who does not wish to see something before them can simply shut their eyes or look away. It is the same with a thought that keeps recurring—you needn't lock eyes with it and wrestle head-on; just move your attention elsewhere.

sections.heading: Method four: slow the momentum behind the thought
paragraphs: The fourth method is subtler. If ignoring them still fails, then attend to "the stilling of the thought-formation" (vitakkasaṅkhārasaṇṭhāna)—notice and slow the force that drives the thoughts along. With this attention, the text says, the evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and fade, and the mind settles into concentration.

The Buddha's simile is a man walking fast: he asks himself, "Why am I walking so fast?" and slows to a walk; asking again, he stands still; again, he sits down; again, he lies down—moving step by step from coarser postures to ever subtler ones. So too with a thought: rather than cutting it off by force, you lower its force and coarseness layer by layer, letting a racing thought slow, loosen, and finally subside of itself.

sections.heading: Method five: restrain mind with mind (last resort)
paragraphs: The fifth and final method is force against force. Only when all four have been tried and the thoughts still cling on does the Buddha teach: "with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the palate, restrain, crush, and beat down the mind with the mind." This is the most forceful measure, driven by sheer will. With this strong restraint, the text says, the evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and fade, and the mind settles into concentration.

The Buddha's simile: a strong man seizes a weaker man by the head, throat, or shoulders and restrains, crushes, and beats him down. Note that this is the finale, not the first choice—its place as the fifth method shows that the gentler methods should be tried first; only when nothing else works does one resort to forcing the thought down by will.

sections.heading: The shared principle, and practical reminders
paragraphs: Set side by side, the five methods share a clear logic. First, the target is always the same class—the "evil, unwholesome thoughts" stirred up by greed, hatred, and delusion. Second, the criterion for success is identical in each case: the thoughts are abandoned and fade, and the mind "settles internally, quiets, becomes unified, and enters concentration." Third, the five are progressive—from switching the object, to seeing the drawbacks, to ignoring, to slowing the momentum, to finally clenching the teeth and suppressing—each more forceful than the last, and if an earlier one works there is no need to invoke a later one.

The text concludes that a monk who can wield the five methods in this way is "a master over the pathways of thought": he thinks whatever thought he wishes, and does not think what he does not wish—having cut off craving, undone the fetters, and made an end of suffering. In practice this gives two reminders: first, don't cling to a single technique—if method A fails, switch to B; that flexibility is exactly how the Buddha designed it. Second, "clenching the teeth and suppressing" is a last resort, not a daily practice; most of the time, switching the object or simply not engaging is enough for the thought to loosen its grip.

en.mahayana_note: These five methods are concrete techniques of meditative practice (samatha-vipassanā). Later Buddhist traditions each developed their own approaches to countering distracting thoughts—for example, reciting a Buddha's name, mantra, visualization, or huatou/kōan inquiry to gather up a scattered mind, or, in modern insight traditions, "noting" the arising and passing of thoughts. These are later developments and interpretations; this page presents only the five steps taught in the Pali text of the Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta, and does not adjudicate among the various methods or their doctrinal orientations.

faq.q: Negative thoughts won't stop—what does Buddhism say to do?
faq.a: The Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta (MN 20) is addressed to exactly this. The Buddha teaches five steps, from mild to forceful: (1) move attention off the object that provokes the bad thought and put a wholesome object in its place; (2) see the drawbacks of the thoughts—they are unwholesome, blameworthy, and result in suffering; (3) simply give them no attention; (4) slow the force that drives the thoughts along; and (5) if nothing else works, clench the teeth and restrain mind with mind by will. If an earlier step works, you don't need the later ones.

faq.q: What are the five methods in the Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta?
faq.a: In the text's order: one, drop the sign that provokes the thought and attend to another sign "connected with the wholesome" (switch the object); two, examine the drawbacks of the thoughts, reflecting "these thoughts are unwholesome, blameworthy, and result in suffering"; three, give the thoughts "no recollection and no attention" (ignore them); four, attend to "the stilling of the thought-formation" (vitakkasaṅkhārasaṇṭhāna—slowing the momentum behind them); five, with teeth clenched and tongue against the palate, "restrain mind with mind" and force it down. The five are used progressively, from gentle to forceful.

faq.q: Too many distracting thoughts in meditation—can I use this?
faq.a: Yes. The discourse is explicitly addressed to one devoted to "the higher mind" (adhicitta—concentration, meditation), precisely for distractions in sitting. When thoughts connected with greed, hatred, or delusion arise on the cushion, work through the steps in order: first switch attention to a wholesome object (for instance return to the breath or a wholesome thought); if that fails, examine the drawbacks of the distractions; if still failing, don't engage them; then slow their force; and only last, restrain them by will. The criterion of success in every case is the same: the thoughts subside and the mind settles, unified, into concentration.

faq.q: I keep dwelling on bad things and unwholesome thoughts won't leave—does that mean something is wrong with me?
faq.a: The text treats thoughts connected with greed, hatred, and delusion as objects to be countered, not as a moral stain—they arise even for a monk cultivating concentration, which is why the Buddha gives five methods for them. In other words, a thought arising doesn't mean you are a bad person; what matters is whether you have a way to handle it. These five steps are a concrete, workable procedure, from gentle to forceful—there is always a method that can loosen the thought's grip.

faq.q: Is there an order to the five methods? Can I use just one?
faq.a: There is a clear order, and it is progressive: each step in the text begins "if, having applied the previous method, the thoughts still arise," before moving on. So if the first method (switching the object) already works—the thoughts subside and the mind settles into concentration—you can use just that and go no further. The later methods are more forceful, and "restraining mind with mind" comes last, reserved for when everything before it has failed.
